chapter_theme: The woman's body as a public record of his absence. Eyes, shoulders and forehead lose their beauty, and each speaker reads that record differently: the friend sees an accusation, the woman refuses to let it be one, and the man, far away and turning for home, sees a reason to hurry.
structure_note: On Parimelazhagar's headnotes, the friend speaks to her in 1231-1235, the woman replies in 1236-1237, and the man, remembering on his way back, speaks in 1238-1240. Manakkudavar gives 1233 and 1234 to the woman, and places the start of the man's speech at 1239, saying three verses begin there.

1231.reading: The friend tells her that as she thinks of the man gone far away, leaving them this misery, her eyes are ashamed before fragrant flowers.

positions.position: He left the pain with them when he went far away, and the friend is the speaker.
positions.quote: இவ்வாற்றாமை நம்கண்ணே நிற்பத் தாம் சேணிடைச் சென்ற காதலரை

positions.position: He went so that their hardship would end, which gives his journey a very different motive.
positions.quote: நமக்குத் துன்பம் ஒழிய வேண்டி, நெடு நெறிக்கண் சென்றாரை

1232.reading: The friend says that her eyes, pale and running with tears, seem to be telling others of the unkindness of the one they desired.
1232.nuance: போலும், 'seem', is doing precise work. Parimelazhagar calls it inference: others deduce what the eyes don't actually say. For the friend, the point is that weeping exposes him, so stop.

1233.reading: Her shoulders, which swelled on the day of union, seem to announce loudly that he has left; the speaker is the friend for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.
1233.nuance: The record needs both moments. Parimelazhagar says those who saw the swelling and now the wasting will quickly work out what happened. It is a before-and-after that is hard to explain away.

positions.position: The friend addresses her: your shoulders are doing what they shouldn't.
The woman speaks to her friend, who has seen her shoulders waste.
positions.quote: பிரிவிடை யாற்றாளாகிய தலைமகள் தனது தோள் வாட்ட முற்றது கண்ட தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

1234.reading: Her shoulders, their old beauty faded with her partner gone, have lost their fullness, and her bright bangles slip; the speaker is the friend for Parimelazhagar and the woman for Manakkudavar.
1234.nuance: தொல்கவின், 'old beauty', matters: for Parimelazhagar she has lost both the beauty he gave and the beauty she had before him. Commentators also differ over the bangle, gold for Parimelazhagar, emerald for Manakkudavar.

positions.position: The friend says these shoulders are betraying his lack of love and his false word.
The woman tells her friend that her shoulders are now thinning as well as losing their beauty.
positions.quote: தோள் அழகழிதலே யன்றி மெலி வதுஞ் செய்யாநின்றதென்று தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

1235.reading: The friend says the shoulders, with bangles lost and old beauty faded, are declaring the cruelty of the cruel one.
1235.nuance: The friend now says openly what 1232-1234 only implied, with both commentators attributing it to her. Manakkudavar gives the purpose: she blames him to help the woman bear up. That prepares the next verse.

1236.reading: The woman tells her friend that with bangles and shoulders slackening, what hurts is hearing him called cruel.
1236.nuance: The friend's strategy has backfired. Parimelazhagar spells out the claim: it's not his absence I can't bear, but what you say. Kalaignar widens the accusers from the friend to anyone who sees her. It's the same defence as in 1190.

1237.reading: The woman asks her heart if it could win any glory by telling the 'cruel' one of the uproar over her wasting shoulders.
1237.nuance: A sardonic challenge. For Parimelazhagar, she says கொடியார் only in quotation, as in 'the one they call cruel'. He reads பூசல் as the friend's blame and her own distress, while Manakkudavar reads it as the town's gossip.

1238.reading: The man remembers that when he once loosened the arms that held her, the forehead of the girl with bright bangles turned pale.
1238.nuance: The voice changes suddenly: we have been with her, and now he is far away and remembering. The conclusion, as Parimelazhagar gives it: if that much did this, what will this absence do? I must go quickly.

positions.position: He loosened his arms out of tenderness, thinking the tight embrace would hurt her.
positions.quote: 'இவட்கு நோம்' என்று கருதி ஒரு ஞான்று யான் நெகிழ்ந்தேனாக

positions.position: He loosened them because he was intending to leave, and she sensed this.
positions.quote: யான் பிரிவதாக நினைத்து, அவள் முயங்கியகைகளை நீக்கினே னாக

1239.reading: The man remembers that when a cool breeze slipped between them in their embrace, the girl's large cool eyes grew pale.
1239.nuance: Parimelazhagar draws the arithmetic: if a breeze could do this, what about mountains, forests and whole countries now between them? Manakkudavar says three verses of the man's speech begin here, which is a different division from Parimelazhagar's.

1240.reading: The man asks whether the pallor in her eyes itself grew distressed on seeing what her bright forehead had done.
1240.nuance: An odd and very ingenious image, and the commentary has to work hard. For Parimelazhagar, the eye's pallor is ashamed because the forehead paled faster, so her parts are competing to lose their beauty, and he should hurry. I find this plausible but can't be sure the verse means that much.

links.note: In 1114, the man says the lily would bow to the ground for shame before her eyes. In 1231, the friend says her eyes are ashamed before flowers. The same flower and the same shame have changed sides, measuring what absence has done.

1108 calls sweet the embrace that even a breeze can't split, using the verb போழ. In 1239 a breeze does split it, with the same verb போழ, and the result is the first sign of her pallor. The ideal of union and its failure are one word apart.

The same incident in two voices: in 1187 she turned slightly in his arms and pallor came, and in 1238 he loosened his arms and her forehead paled. In her telling it happens to her, and in his it is what he did.

source_issues: 1231: Pope's prose is cut off mid-word ('and shun (the').
1233: Parimelazhagar's entry ends with a stray underscore before ---.

1239: Manakkudavar's count of 'three verses from here' for the man doesn't match the chapter's end at 1240, unless his order differs from this one. 1238 is also in the man's voice in his gloss, which suggests a misplaced note.
